scenes.narration: One hundred and eighteen billion dollars. That is roughly how much the United States Postal Service has lost since twenty oh six, according to the Government Accountability Office.

And it keeps going. The Postal Service lost nine point five billion dollars in twenty twenty-four, and nine billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. On the day this video was made, it reported a loss of six point five billion dollars for twenty twenty-six.
So how does an organization that delivers to every address in America keep losing money? And who pays for it?

By the end of this video, you will know what the Postal Service has to do by law, how a law from twenty oh six turned into a giant bill, why the letter is disappearing, and why the money is running out of room.

scenes.narration: Start with the job. The Postal Service delivers to more than one hundred and seventy million addresses, six and often seven days a week. In twenty twenty-five alone, about one point eight million new addresses were added to its routes. Every new house, every new apartment, is one more stop.

The machine behind that is enormous. According to the Postal Service, it runs about two hundred and thirty-six thousand delivery routes, nearly thirty-one thousand retail offices, and a fleet of more than two hundred and sixty thousand vehicles. Every one of those vehicles has to keep moving, whether the mail grows or not.

And here is the part many people get wrong. The Postal Service generally receives no tax dollars for its operating expenses. It is supposed to pay its own way, by selling stamps, delivering packages and charging for mail.

But it cannot run like a normal company. By law, it must deliver at least six days a week. It must serve a farm at the end of a dirt road as well as an office tower in a big city. That promise is called universal service.

That promise has a cost that does not shrink when the mail shrinks. A carrier still has to drive the whole route, whether the bag holds fifty letters or five. The network is fixed. The revenue is not.

Let me draw the problem. Here is a route with ten houses. Each day, the carrier visits every one. Now the letters fall by half. The route stays the same. Same truck, same miles, same time. Fewer letters to pay for each stop.

scenes.narration: That alone would make life hard. But in twenty oh six, Congress added something much bigger.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The Postal Accountability and Enhancement Act set fixed payments for the health care of future retirees. Every year for ten years, the Postal Service had to put roughly five and a half billion dollars a year into a fund for workers who had not yet retired. By our sum, about fifty-six billion dollars over the decade.

Those were fixed amounts, written into the law, whatever happened to the business. And they arrived just as the mail started its long decline. The Postal Service soon stopped making them, and the missed payments kept piling up on its books as losses.

In twenty twenty-two, Congress tried to fix it. The Postal Service Reform Act canceled fifty-seven billion dollars of missed payments. It also moved postal retirees onto Medicare, which cut the retiree health bill by about sixty-one billion dollars. And it wrote the six-day delivery rule directly into law.

But the reform did not end the bills. The Postal Service still owes payments for pensions, and new top-up payments for retiree health, about seven hundred and fifty million dollars in twenty twenty-six, growing to about one point four billion by fiscal year twenty thirty-one, according to the auditors. The government's auditors expect that health fund to run dry in fiscal year twenty thirty-one.

Let me draw the bill. Here is the Postal Service. Here is the fund for future retirees. Every year, a big arrow of money was supposed to flow into it. When the arrow stopped, the debt grew. In twenty twenty-two, Congress erased much of it. But a smaller arrow is still there.

scenes.narration: The retiree bills explain part of the losses. The rest comes from something you can see in your own mailbox.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: First-Class Mail, the letters and bills that once paid for the whole system, peaked in twenty oh one. That year, the Postal Service handled about one hundred and four billion pieces of it. In twenty twenty-six, it handled about forty billion. Counting every kind of mail, the total peaked a few years later, in twenty oh six, at more than two hundred and thirteen billion pieces. It has been falling ever since.

Here is the most striking number. In twenty oh seven, each delivery point received about five and a half pieces of mail a day. In twenty twenty-six, it was two point three. More stops, and much less in the bag at each one.

Packages are the bright spot. In twenty twenty-six, shipping and packages brought in thirty-four point one billion dollars, more than the twenty-six point two billion dollars from First-Class Mail. In twenty twenty-five, the Postal Service said its revenue grew mostly thanks to its Ground Advantage shipping service. But packages are a competitive business. Private carriers fight for the same customers, so the Postal Service cannot simply raise prices.

On letters, it has raised prices, again and again. A Forever stamp cost fifty-five cents in twenty nineteen. Since July twenty twenty-six, it costs eighty-two cents. By our calculation, that is about forty-nine percent more in seven years.

Let me draw the two lines. Here is the letter line, starting high in twenty oh one and falling year after year. Here is the stamp price line, starting low and climbing. When fewer people buy something, raising the price only works for so long.

scenes.narration: In twenty twenty-one, the Postal Service announced a plan to turn all of this around.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: It was called Delivering for America, a ten-year plan. It promised to break even by fiscal year twenty twenty-three, and to avoid one hundred and sixty billion dollars in projected losses over ten years. It also promised forty billion dollars of investment and better on-time delivery.

Break-even never came. The government's auditors found that from twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-four, revenue was actually about twenty-four billion dollars higher than the plan expected. But expenses were about thirty-six billion dollars higher. The costs ran faster than the sales.

The twenty twenty-six loss looked smaller, but read the fine print. Much of the improvement came from accounting for workers' compensation, which moves with interest rates. That one line swung by about two point four billion dollars. The loss the Postal Service says it can actually control was still more than two billion dollars. In twenty twenty-five, that controllable loss was about two point seven billion.

Let me draw the gap. Here is the revenue the plan expected. Here is what actually came in, a little higher. Now here are the expected costs, and here are the real costs, much higher. The plan beat its sales target and still lost, because the costs grew even faster.

scenes.narration: Which leads to the most serious problem of all. The Postal Service is running out of room to borrow.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The Postal Service can borrow from the Treasury, but only up to a legal limit of fifteen billion dollars. That limit has not changed since nineteen ninety-two. And the Postal Service has already reached it.

keyframes.cue: only up to a legal limit

scenes.narration: So in twenty twenty-six, it started skipping bills. With a waiver from its regulator, it did not make its pension payments for the year. It paused some employer pension contributions. And in its own words, it defaulted on a seven hundred and twenty-six million dollar payment for retiree health.

The long-term gaps are huge. The Postal Service reports ninety-seven point one billion dollars in unfunded pension obligations, and about forty-four billion dollars more for retiree health. The government's auditors have kept its finances on their high-risk list since twenty oh nine, and say Congress should act now.

Let me draw the squeeze. On one side, a fixed network that grows every year. On another, letters that keep falling. On top, retiree bills that never go away. And underneath, a credit line already at its limit. Four walls, closing in at once.

scenes.narration: So why does the Post Office keep losing billions? Because it is asked to run like a business and serve like a public utility at the same time. It must reach every address, six days a week, while its most profitable product disappears and old promises to retirees come due. Until Congress decides who pays for that promise, the losses are the bill. Every stamp, every package and every new address on a route is part of that same calculation. And for now, the bill keeps arriving, six days a week.
